description: Most trend tools stop at the surface. Lapse maps how the atmosphere is changing at every height and tests whether each change is real. Warming below, cooling above, one cause. Join us if you love Earth science, statistics, or data visualization.
summary:
Everyone asks whether the planet is warming. The honest answer depends on how high you look.

Lapse turns 24 years of NASA's AIRS satellite record and 47 years of the MERRA-2 reanalysis into one climb. Scroll, and the page rises from the ground to 48 km while the height, the rate of change and the colour change with you. Averaged over the globe, the air is warming low down (+0.27 °C per ten years near 8 km) and cooling more than twice as fast higher up (-0.59 °C per ten years near 32 km). The direction flips near 19 km.

Every height carries one of four plain labels: Clear change, Likely change, Not proven yet, or Disputed. The labels come from rules, not opinion: a statistical test, a second independent dataset, a check that removes volcano months, and a check for jumps when a data source changed.

Visitors can also ask questions in their own words. Every number in an answer is checked against the NASA results before it is shown.

It matters because the surface is only the bottom of the story. In 1967 physicists predicted that rising carbon dioxide would warm the air below and cool the air above. NASA's records show that pattern. Lapse lets anyone see it, check it, and see how sure we are.
details:
What it does

Lapse is a website about how the air is changing at every height, built for people with no science background. It opens with the finding in four words: "Warming below. Cooling above."

  • The ascent. Scroll, drag the column or press Play, and the page rises from the ground to the top of the record. At each measured height it shows the rate of change, a plain label and one sentence. The colours follow the direction: warm where the air is warming, cool where it is cooling. Familiar heights are marked, such as Mount Everest and where airliners cruise.
  • Guess first. One question before the climb: which is changing faster, the warming below or the cooling above?
  • Above you. Share a location or type a city, and the climb replays for the band of sky at that latitude.
  • Ask the data. A question box that answers only from the NASA results. Every number in an answer is checked against them before it is shown.
  • Three cases and the evidence. Guided demonstrations (one cause with opposite trends, a volcano in the record, a jump in a data source) and three charts of the same measurements: every latitude and height, every height at one place, and the month-by-month history with known events shaded.
  • Investigate it yourself. Every data source, method and check in one place, with a table that shows whether the method changes the answer.

Air temperature, water vapor and ozone are available, for the whole globe, five regions or any five-degree band of latitude.

How it works

A Python pipeline reads NASA's AIRS and MERRA-2 monthly data, averages it in five-degree bands of latitude at every pressure level, removes the seasonal cycle, and computes a trend (Theil-Sen slope with a 95% range) and a significance test (Mann-Kendall, corrected for month-to-month memory, with false discovery control). Each result gets one of four labels by rule:

  • Clear change: two independent datasets both pass the test, in the same direction, with overlapping ranges.
  • Likely change: one dataset passes the test and nothing contradicts it.
  • Not proven yet: the change cannot be told apart from chance. This is not "no change".
  • Disputed: the second dataset shows the opposite, the trend depends on volcano months, or the record jumps when its data source changed.

The t-test, the Mann-Kendall test and confidence intervals named in the challenge are all offered as interchangeable tools. On made-up records with no trend, the three sound methods raise a false alarm 3 to 8 times in 100. The plain textbook test does 30 to 65, so it is shown for comparison only.

The question box can only call eleven read-only tools over the published results, and a program rejects any answer containing a number that no tool produced. With no language model connected it still answers, by rule.

How it meets the challenge

  • Select variables: air temperature, water vapor and ozone, each with a one-line definition.
  • Where: the whole globe, five regions, or any five-degree band, at up to 42 heights.
  • Visualize change over time: a month-by-month history for any place and height.
  • How much, and is it significant: a rate with its range, a test, and a plain label.
  • Opposite trends from one process: the challenge's central idea, shown in one column of air and listed automatically for every region.

What is creative, and what we considered

Height is the angle. The challenge mentions trends at "levels of the atmosphere", and of about twenty public entries we found for this challenge, none works on them. Labels can say "we don't know", with the reason. The jump check caught a known problem by itself: MERRA-2 above about 40 km steps by several degrees when its input satellites changed. The finding itself is known science, predicted in 1967 and found in satellite records by a 2023 study. What Lapse adds is a way for anyone to see it in half a minute and check every number behind it.

Five published results were checked on the same years and heights, and four match. For example, above about 36 km for 2003 to 2012 the published cooling is 0.65 K per decade and ours is 0.65. Every published number can be recomputed from the repository with one command and no NASA login, and 88 automated tests run on every change.

Limits

Values are averages around the whole Earth at one latitude, not local. A trend shows what changed, not why. Heights in km are converted from pressure and are approximate. Water vapor and ozone rest on one dataset, so they can never be labelled "Clear change".

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, xarray, netCDF4, requests, pytest). Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework; the charts are drawn on Canvas and SVG. GitHub Actions for tests, Vercel for hosting. Most of the code and text were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude) that the team directed and checked, and the question box uses Google Gemini to phrase answers. The demo video is a screen recording of the site with our own voice. Code: https://github.com/lazizbekravshanov/lapse

When it was built

Work began the evening before the event (repository, NASA download code, a first page on real data). The rest was built during the event.
dataRefs: AIRS3STM v7.0: Aqua/AIRS Level 3 monthly standard retrieval, 1 degree (air temperature, 2002 to 2026)
M2IMNPASM v5.12.4: MERRA-2 monthly means on 42 pressure levels (temperature, water vapor, ozone, 1980 to 2026)
NASA Common Metadata Repository (CMR): used to find the data files
NASA GES DISC: the data archive, read over OPeNDAP with an Earthdata login
NASA JPL AIRS project: published temperature trends we check our numbers against
projectRefs: Manabe and Wetherald 1967, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences: the prediction of warming below and cooling above
Santer and others 2023, PNAS: the pattern found in satellite records
Pan and others 2017, Journal of Climate: temperature change in the upper air, 2003 to 2012
Davis and others 2017, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics: where reanalysis water vapor can be trusted
Claude by Anthropic: AI coding assistant used to write most of the code and text
Google Gemini API: phrases the answers in the ask box
Model Context Protocol: lets outside AI assistants use the same read-only tools
Playwright: recording the site for the demo video
faster-whisper: finding word times in the voice recording to place the subtitles
Inter typeface: subtitles and end card of the demo video
